content: To evaluate the duration of bedaquiline (BDQ) treatment, we anticipate approximately 20 patients over a span of zero days. Variations in treatment duration must be considered. Therefore, we propose analyzing the frequency distribution of BDQ treatment durations to identify inter-modal cut-off points that best distinguish patients treated for 24 weeks, 36 weeks, or 52 weeks. To define these cut-off points, we will exclude patients who died or were lost to follow-up, ensuring the analysis focuses on those who could have received the drug for the specified durations. This approach will also be applied to the sensitivity analysis population. It is important to acknowledge that any selected time point will inevitably dichotomize some patients who received only slightly different durations of BDQ treatment. However, by selecting inter-modal points, this issue should be minimized. Step 1: Descriptive Analysis of Population Subgroups We will conduct a descriptive analysis to characterize patients who did not receive BDQ, those who received BDQ for at least one month but less than six months, and those who received BDQ for at least 24 weeks. The latter group will be further divided into two subgroups: those treated for exactly 24 weeks and those treated for more than 24 weeks. Among the latter, we will also distinguish between patients treated for 24–36 weeks and those treated for more than 36 weeks. The analysis will include details such as the treatment site, baseline/pre-treatment characteristics (e.g., sex, age, HIV status, antiretroviral therapy use, comorbidities, prior tuberculosis treatment, acid-fast bacilli smear results, chest X-ray findings, drug susceptibility testing results, year of treatment initiation, and the number of likely effective drugs initially used). The total number of drugs to which a patient is resistant will also be considered, as greater resistance limits treatment options and increases the likelihood of BDQ extension. This covariate will be adjusted for in the statistical analysis. Step 2: Exploring Delamanid Use We will similarly analyze the characteristics of patients who received delamanid (DLM) without BDQ, those who did not receive DLM, and those who received both DLM and BDQ. We will examine whether DLM was used from the start of treatment or introduced later, as many patients received DLM after several months of therapy. This raises the possibility of indication bias (e.g., DLM added for poor responders) and immortal time bias (patients must survive longer to receive DLM later). Median time to DLM initiation after treatment start will be described, along with the proportion of patients starting DLM within specific time intervals (e.g., 0–3 months, 4–6 months, etc.). We will also assess whether patient characteristics were balanced between treatment groups and adjust for DLM use in multivariable analyses. Step 3: Analysis of BDQ Duration To assess the benefit of extending BDQ treatment beyond 24 weeks, we will employ two analytical methods and compare the results for each of the four defined outcomes. These methods will also be repeated for sensitivity analyses. The first method involves exact and propensity score matching, where baseline characteristics (e.g., drug resistance patterns, HIV status, age, sex, etc.) and during-treatment characteristics (e.g., culture status, acquired resistance, adverse events, etc.) will be used for matching. The second method involves survival analysis using inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) and censor weighting (IPCW). more than six months) and continuously (duration of BDQ beyond six months). The primary outcome will be a composite of failure, relapse, or death, with loss to follow-up treated as a censoring event. Question 2: Improved Outcomes with Extended BDQ Use We will analyze whether treatment outcomes improve in patients receiving more than six months of BDQ compared to those receiving no BDQ or six months of BDQ. Patients will be matched on baseline characteristics (e.g., drug resistance, HIV status, country income level) and further matched using propensity scores for other variables (e.g., age, sex, prior treatment, disease extent, etc.). Due to limitations in detailed therapy data, changes and events during treatment cannot be included in this analysis. Question 3: Combined IPD-2019 and EndTB Data Analysis Using combined datasets, we will assess whether extended BDQ use improves outcomes compared to no BDQ or six months of BDQ. The analysis will follow the same approach as Question 2, comparing reference groups to those receiving BDQ for 24 weeks or more than 24 weeks. Adverse events will also be analyzed, focusing on the proportion of patients permanently stopping drugs due to adverse events and the types of events observed. Question 4: Concomitant Use of BDQ and DLM We will evaluate whether the combined use of BDQ and DLM improves outcomes compared to other treatment regimens. Challenges include variability in DLM use across sites and its introduction later in therapy. A descriptive analysis will compare patients receiving BDQ and DLM to those receiving only BDQ or DLM. Statistical analyses will compare outcomes between these groups, focusing on treatment success, bacteriological cure, adherence, failure, relapse, survival, and adverse events. Patients receiving prolonged BDQ or DLM may have been sicker or had fewer treatment options, potentially underestimating the benefit of these drugs. Sensitivity analyses will address missed doses, time to loss to follow-up, and the effect of specific drugs in the regimen. Additionally, the analysis of adverse events may be limited by incomplete data on drug duration and severity grading.
